From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NSA_scotland_map_opengov.pngA map of the National Scenic Areas of Scotland
National scenic area (NSA) is a [conservation designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_designation) used in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland), and administered by [NatureScot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NatureScot) on behalf of the [Scottish Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Government). The designation's purpose is to identify areas of exceptional scenery and to protect them from inappropriate development. There are currently 40 national scenic areas (NSAs) in Scotland, covering 13% of the land area of Scotland.[[1]](#cite_note-SNH-1) The areas protected by the designation are considered to represent the type of scenic beauty "popularly associated with Scotland and for which it is renowned".[[2]](#cite_note-2) As such they tend to be mainly found in remote and mountainous areas,[[1]](#cite_note-SNH-1) with a review in 1997 noting a potential weakness of national scenic areas was that the original selection placed undue emphasis on [mountainous parts of the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountains_and_hills_of_Scotland).[[3]](#cite_note-SNH1997-3) National scenic areas do however also cover seascapes, with approximately 26% of the total area protected by the designation being marine.[[4]](#cite_note-area-4) The designation is primarily concerned with scenic qualities, although designated national scenic areas may well have other special qualities, for example related to culture, history, archaeology, geology or wildlife. Areas with such qualities may be protected by other designations (e.g. [national nature reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_nature_reserve_(Scotland))) that overlap with the NSA designation.[[5]](#cite_note-qualities-5)
National scenic areas are designated by the [IUCN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN) as Category V Protected Landscapes, the same international category as [Scotland's two national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_Scotland).[[1]](#cite_note-SNH-1) Within the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom) the NSA designation is regarded as equivalent to the [Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty) (AONBs) of [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England), [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales) and [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland).[[1]](#cite_note-SNH-1)

The national scenic area designation does not have a high profile when compared to other [conservation designations used in Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_areas_of_Scotland): in 2018 a survey by the [National Trust for Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Trust_for_Scotland) found that only 20% of Scots were "definitely aware" of national scenic areas, compared to 80% for National Parks.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Main_ridge_of_the_cuillin_in_skye_arp.jpgThe [Cuillin Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuillin) national scenic area.
After the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War), the [Labour government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attlee_ministry) passed the [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949), which led to the creation of ten [national parks in England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_England_and_Wales) between 1951 and 1957, although no parks were created in Scotland. A committee, chaired by Sir Douglas Ramsay, was however established to consider preservation of the landscape in Scotland. The report, published in 1945, proposed that five areas (Loch Lomond & the Trossachs, the Cairngorms, Glen Coe-Ben Nevis-Black Mount, Wester Ross and Glen Strathfarrar-Glen Affric-Glen Cannich) should receive a level of protection.[[7]](#cite_note-cairngom-history-7) Accordingly, the government designated these areas as "national park direction areas", giving powers for planning decisions taken by local authorities to be reviewed by central government. After a further review of landscape protection in 1978, additional areas were identified for protection, and in 1981 the direction areas were replaced by national scenic areas, which were based on the 1978 recommendations.[[3]](#cite_note-SNH1997-3)

Following the passage of the [National Parks (Scotland) Act 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_(Scotland)_Act_2000), two [national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks) were established: [Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park) and the [Cairngorms National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park).[[8]](#cite_note-8) Both of these parks included areas that were already designated as national scenic areas, and the NSA designation remains in place alongside national park status for the areas in question.

[Scottish Natural Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NatureScot) reviewed the national scenic areas between November 2007 and March 2009 to try to identify what makes the scenery of each NSA special;[[5]](#cite_note-qualities-5) however no formal review into the number and extent has been undertaken since the original report. The current national scenic areas, which therefore remain as originally mapped in 1978, were legally redesignated in 2010.[[9]](#cite_note-policy-9) Despite calls from bodies such as the [John Muir Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Muir_Trust) for the protection to be extended to other areas to protect landscape and support tourism, the Scottish Government has stated that it has no plans to designate further areas. In September 2017 the Scottish Parliament's Public Petitions Committee asked the government to explain why it is not reviewing the NSAs.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kyles-of-bute-2013-10-12.jpgThe [Kyles of Bute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyles_of_Bute) national scenic area in [Argyll and Bute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyll_and_Bute).
NSAs are currently designated under the [Planning etc. (Scotland) Act 2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_etc._(Scotland)_Act_2006): all 40 current NSAs were redesignated under this act via a single order in 2010.[[9]](#cite_note-policy-9) Designation provides an additional level of protection to specified areas. For developments that would ordinarily require only [local authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdivisions_of_Scotland) planning permission the [Scottish Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Government) must be informed if advice from NatureScot is ignored.[[11]](#cite_note-planning-11) Additionally, there are some classes of development that would not normally require planning permission to proceed when located outwith a national scenic area, but which are subject to controls within them. These developments include the erection of agricultural and forestry buildings over 12 m high, the construction of vehicle tracks for agriculture or forestry purposes (unless forming part of an approved scheme), and local authority roadworks outside present road boundaries costing more than £100,000.[[11]](#cite_note-planning-11) The NSA designation has thus served to prevent major intrusive developments such as wind farms occurring within the designated areas.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

There is no equivalent to a [national park authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park_authority) for national scenic areas, as controls on development are exercised through the [planning system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_permission_in_the_United_Kingdom). Local authorities can produce a management strategy for each of the NSA within its territory. This strategy defines the area's special qualities and identifies the actions needed to safeguard them. As of 2018, only the three national scenic areas within [Dumfries and Galloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumfries_and_Galloway) have current management strategies .[[13]](#cite_note-13)

Public access to all land in Scotland is governed by the [Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Reform_(Scotland)_Act_2003), which grants the public a [right of responsible access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_to_roam) to most land (and water) for activities such as [walking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiking), [camping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camping), [cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling), [canoeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canoeing), [swimming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming) and [climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing); this right applies to land regardless of ownership or whether or not it is in a designated or protected area such as an NSA, providing it is exercised responsibly (as defined by the [Scottish Outdoor Access Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Outdoor_Access_Code)).[[14]](#cite_note-14)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NSA_scotland_map_opengov.pngA map of the National Scenic Areas of Scotland
National scenic area (NSA) is a [conservation designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_designation) used in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland), and administered by [NatureScot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NatureScot) on behalf of the [Scottish Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Government). The designation's purpose is to identify areas of exceptional scenery and to protect them from inappropriate development. There are currently 40 national scenic areas (NSAs) in Scotland, covering 13% of the land area of Scotland.[[1]](#cite_note-SNH-1) The areas protected by the designation are considered to represent the type of scenic beauty "popularly associated with Scotland and for which it is renowned".[[2]](#cite_note-2) As such they tend to be mainly found in remote and mountainous areas,[[1]](#cite_note-SNH-1) with a review in 1997 noting a potential weakness of national scenic areas was that the original selection placed undue emphasis on [mountainous parts of the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountains_and_hills_of_Scotland).[[3]](#cite_note-SNH1997-3) National scenic areas do however also cover seascapes, with approximately 26% of the total area protected by the designation being marine.[[4]](#cite_note-area-4) The designation is primarily concerned with scenic qualities, although designated national scenic areas may well have other special qualities, for example related to culture, history, archaeology, geology or wildlife. Areas with such qualities may be protected by other designations (e.g. [national nature reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_nature_reserve_(Scotland))) that overlap with the NSA designation.[[5]](#cite_note-qualities-5)
National scenic areas are designated by the [IUCN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN) as Category V Protected Landscapes, the same international category as [Scotland's two national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_Scotland).[[1]](#cite_note-SNH-1) Within the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom) the NSA designation is regarded as equivalent to the [Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty) (AONBs) of [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England), [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales) and [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland).[[1]](#cite_note-SNH-1)

The national scenic area designation does not have a high profile when compared to other [conservation designations used in Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_areas_of_Scotland): in 2018 a survey by the [National Trust for Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Trust_for_Scotland) found that only 20% of Scots were "definitely aware" of national scenic areas, compared to 80% for National Parks.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Main_ridge_of_the_cuillin_in_skye_arp.jpgThe [Cuillin Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuillin) national scenic area.
After the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War), the [Labour government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attlee_ministry) passed the [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949), which led to the creation of ten [national parks in England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_England_and_Wales) between 1951 and 1957, although no parks were created in Scotland. A committee, chaired by Sir Douglas Ramsay, was however established to consider preservation of the landscape in Scotland. The report, published in 1945, proposed that five areas (Loch Lomond & the Trossachs, the Cairngorms, Glen Coe-Ben Nevis-Black Mount, Wester Ross and Glen Strathfarrar-Glen Affric-Glen Cannich) should receive a level of protection.[[7]](#cite_note-cairngom-history-7) Accordingly, the government designated these areas as "national park direction areas", giving powers for planning decisions taken by local authorities to be reviewed by central government. After a further review of landscape protection in 1978, additional areas were identified for protection, and in 1981 the direction areas were replaced by national scenic areas, which were based on the 1978 recommendations.[[3]](#cite_note-SNH1997-3)

Following the passage of the [National Parks (Scotland) Act 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_(Scotland)_Act_2000), two [national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks) were established: [Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park) and the [Cairngorms National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park).[[8]](#cite_note-8) Both of these parks included areas that were already designated as national scenic areas, and the NSA designation remains in place alongside national park status for the areas in question.

[Scottish Natural Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NatureScot) reviewed the national scenic areas between November 2007 and March 2009 to try to identify what makes the scenery of each NSA special;[[5]](#cite_note-qualities-5) however no formal review into the number and extent has been undertaken since the original report. The current national scenic areas, which therefore remain as originally mapped in 1978, were legally redesignated in 2010.[[9]](#cite_note-policy-9) Despite calls from bodies such as the [John Muir Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Muir_Trust) for the protection to be extended to other areas to protect landscape and support tourism, the Scottish Government has stated that it has no plans to designate further areas. In September 2017 the Scottish Parliament's Public Petitions Committee asked the government to explain why it is not reviewing the NSAs.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kyles-of-bute-2013-10-12.jpgThe [Kyles of Bute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyles_of_Bute) national scenic area in [Argyll and Bute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyll_and_Bute).
NSAs are currently designated under the [Planning etc. (Scotland) Act 2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_etc._(Scotland)_Act_2006): all 40 current NSAs were redesignated under this act via a single order in 2010.[[9]](#cite_note-policy-9) Designation provides an additional level of protection to specified areas. For developments that would ordinarily require only [local authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdivisions_of_Scotland) planning permission the [Scottish Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Government) must be informed if advice from NatureScot is ignored.[[11]](#cite_note-planning-11) Additionally, there are some classes of development that would not normally require planning permission to proceed when located outwith a national scenic area, but which are subject to controls within them. These developments include the erection of agricultural and forestry buildings over 12 m high, the construction of vehicle tracks for agriculture or forestry purposes (unless forming part of an approved scheme), and local authority roadworks outside present road boundaries costing more than £100,000.[[11]](#cite_note-planning-11) The NSA designation has thus served to prevent major intrusive developments such as wind farms occurring within the designated areas.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

There is no equivalent to a [national park authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park_authority) for national scenic areas, as controls on development are exercised through the [planning system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_permission_in_the_United_Kingdom). Local authorities can produce a management strategy for each of the NSA within its territory. This strategy defines the area's special qualities and identifies the actions needed to safeguard them. As of 2018, only the three national scenic areas within [Dumfries and Galloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumfries_and_Galloway) have current management strategies .[[13]](#cite_note-13)

Public access to all land in Scotland is governed by the [Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Reform_(Scotland)_Act_2003), which grants the public a [right of responsible access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_to_roam) to most land (and water) for activities such as [walking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiking), [camping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camping), [cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling), [canoeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canoeing), [swimming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming) and [climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing); this right applies to land regardless of ownership or whether or not it is in a designated or protected area such as an NSA, providing it is exercised responsibly (as defined by the [Scottish Outdoor Access Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Outdoor_Access_Code)).[[14]](#cite_note-14)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:England_and_Wales_National_Landscapes_map.svgNational Landscapes in [England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_and_Wales)

A National Landscape ([Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_language): Tirwedd Cenedlaethol), formally and formerly an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB; [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_language): Ardal o Harddwch Naturiol Eithriadol, AHNE), is one of 38 areas of [countryside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_area) in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England) and [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales) that has been designated for [conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_area) due to its significant landscape value. The current name was adopted in 2023.

Areas are designated in recognition of their national importance by the relevant public body: [Natural England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_England) or [Natural Resources Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Resources_Wales), respectively. On 22 November 2023, following a review, the AONBs in England and Wales adopted the National Landscapes name, and are in the process of rebranding. The name "area of outstanding natural beauty" is still the designated legal term.

[Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland) has eight areas that maintain the name "[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty_(Northern_Ireland))", as the renaming did not apply to Northern Ireland which is under different legislation. Scotland uses the similar [national scenic area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_scenic_area_(Scotland)) (NSA) designation.

National Landscapes enjoy levels of protection from development similar to those of [UK national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_the_United_Kingdom), but unlike national parks the responsible bodies do not have their own [planning powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_and_country_planning_in_the_United_Kingdom). They also differ from national parks in their more limited opportunities for extensive outdoor recreation.[[1]](#cite_note-Gov-1)

There are 38 National Landscapes, 33 wholly in England, [four wholly in Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Landscapes_in_Wales) and [one on the England–Wales border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wye_Valley_National_Landscape), as well as a further eight AONBs in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland).

The idea for what would eventually become the AONB designation was first put forward by [John Dower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gordon_Dower) in his 1945 Report to the Government on National Parks in England and Wales. Dower suggested there was need for protection of certain naturally beautiful landscapes that were unsuitable as national parks owing to their small size and lack of wildness. Dower's recommendation for the designation of these "other amenity areas" was eventually embodied in the [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949) as the AONB designation.[[2]](#cite_note-AONB_story-2)

The purpose of an AONB designation in England and Wales is to [conserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landscape-scale_conservation) and enhance the natural beauty of the designated landscape.[[1]](#cite_note-Gov-1)

There are two secondary aims: meeting the need for quiet enjoyment of the countryside and having regard for the interests of those who live and work there. To achieve these aims, AONBs rely on [planning controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_and_country_planning_in_the_United_Kingdom) and practical countryside management. As they have the same landscape quality, AONBs may be compared to the [national parks of England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_England_and_Wales). National parks are well known in the UK; by contrast, there is evidence to indicate many residents in AONBs may be unaware of the status. However, the National Association of AONBs launched initiatives to increase awareness of AONBs in local communities,[[3]](#cite_note-3) and, in 2014, successfully negotiated to have the boundaries of AONBs in England shown on [Google Maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Maps).[[4]](#cite_note-4)

## Statistical overview
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=National_Landscape&action=edit&section=3)]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ThreeCliffsBay.jos.500pix.jpgView over [Three Cliffs Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Cliffs_Bay) in the [Gower Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gower_Peninsula), the first designated Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty
There are 48 "Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty" in the United Kingdom in total, 33 in England, [four in Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areas_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty_in_Wales), [one on the England–Wales border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wye_Valley_AONB), and a further eight AONBs in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland). Those in England and Wales are branded as "National Landscapes".

The first AONB was established in 1956 on the [Gower Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gower_Peninsula) in [South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Wales), and the most recent to be designated is the [Tamar Valley AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamar_Valley_AONB), established in 1995.[[5]](#cite_note-5) More recent changes include the Clwydian Range AONB being extended in 2012 to form the [Clwydian Range and Dee Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clwydian_Range_and_Dee_Valley) AONB, and in Northern Ireland, the [Strangford Lough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangford_Lough) and [Lecale Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale_Coast_AONB) AONBs were merged to form a single AONB in 2010.[[6]](#cite_note-strangfordandlecale-6)

AONBs vary greatly in terms of size, type and use of land, and whether they are partly or wholly open to the public. The smallest AONB is the [Isles of Scilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isles_of_Scilly), 16 km2 (6.2 sq mi), and the largest is the [Cotswolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotswolds),[[7]](#cite_note-7) 2,038 km2 (787 sq mi). AONBs cover around 15% of England and 4% of Wales.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

## Legal status and organisation
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=National_Landscape&action=edit&section=4)]

Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in [England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_and_Wales) (now also National Landscapes) were originally created under the same legislation as the [national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park), the [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949). Unlike AONBs, national parks have special legal powers to prevent unsympathetic development. AONBs in general remain the responsibility of their local authorities by means of special committees that include members appointed by a [minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_(United_Kingdom)) and by parishes, and only very limited statutory duties were imposed on local authorities within an AONB by the original 1949 Act. However, further regulation and protection of AONBs in England and Wales was added by the [Countryside and Rights of Way (CRoW) Act 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countryside_and_Rights_of_Way_Act_2000), under which new designations are now made,[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

In the [National Planning Policy Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Planning_Policy_Framework) (March 2012), the government stated that AONBs and national parks have equal status when it comes to planning decisions on landscape issues. Two of the AONBs (the Cotswolds and the Chilterns), which extend into a large number of local authority areas, have their own statutory bodies, known as conservation boards. In 2019, the [Glover Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Glover_(journalist)) made various recommendations regarding the future of AONBs – the report's 'central proposal' being to bring [National Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_the_United_Kingdom) and AONBs together as part of one 'family of national landscapes'.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Following the report the Cotswolds Conservation Board announced in September 2020 that they were re-styling the area name and it is now known as the Cotswolds National Landscape.[[12]](#cite_note-12) The UK Government later accepted the report's recommendation for the AONBs in England to use "National Landscape".[[13]](#cite_note-13)

All English and Welsh AONBs have a dedicated AONB officer and other staff. As required by the CRoW Act, each AONB has a management plan that sets out the characteristics and special qualities of the landscape and how they will be conserved and enhanced. The AONBs are collectively represented by the "National Landscapes Association",[[14]](#cite_note-14) previously the "National Association for Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty" (NAAONB), an independent registered charity in England and Wales[[15]](#cite_note-15) acting on behalf of AONBs and their partners, which had used the slogan "Landscapes for Life".[[16]](#cite_note-aaonb-16)

AONBs in Northern Ireland are designated under separate legislation, originally under the Amenity Lands (NI) Act 1965; later replaced by the Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (NI) Order 1985.[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-:19-18)[[19]](#cite_note-:2-19) The [Northern Ireland Environment Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Environment_Agency) (part of the [Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Agriculture,_Environment_and_Rural_Affairs)[[20]](#cite_note-20) of the [Northern Ireland Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Executive)) is responsible for designating AONBs in Northern Ireland, and facilitates their management.[[21]](#cite_note-:7-21)

On 22 November 2023, following a 2022 Landscapes Review policy paper by [Julian Glover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Glover_(journalist)),[[22]](#cite_note-22) the AONBs in England and Wales adopted the National Landscapes name, and subsequently rebranded.[[23]](#cite_note-nlwelcome-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24) The name "area of outstanding natural beauty" is still the designated legal term.[[25]](#cite_note-25) The review did not extend to Northern Ireland, and its AONBs did not adopt the new name.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Amexstadjuly10.jpg[Falmer Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falmer_Stadium) under construction in 2010 in the former [Sussex Downs AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex_Downs_AONB)
There are growing concerns among environmental and countryside groups that AONB status is increasingly under threat from development. The [Campaign to Protect Rural England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_to_Protect_Rural_England) said in July 2006 that many AONBs were under greater threat than ever before.[[27]](#cite_note-27) Three particular AONBs were cited: the [Dorset AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorset_AONB) threatened by a road plan, the threat of a football stadium in the [Sussex Downs AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex_Downs_AONB), and, larger than any other, a £1 billion plan by [Imperial College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_College_London) to build thousands of houses and offices on hundreds of acres of AONB land on the [Kent Downs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_Downs) at [Wye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wye,_Kent).[[28]](#cite_note-28) The plan was eventually abandoned in 2006 after sustained local opposition. However, in September 2007 government approval was finally given for the development of a new football ground for [Brighton and Hove Albion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton_and_Hove_Albion) within the boundaries of the Sussex Downs AONB, after a fierce fight by conservationists. The subsequent development, known as [Falmer Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falmer_Stadium), was officially opened in July 2011. The Weymouth Relief Road in Dorset was constructed between 2008 and 2011, after environmental groups lost a High Court challenge to prevent its construction.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

Writing in 2006, Professor Adrian Phillips listed threats facing AONBs, which he says include uncertainty over future support for land management, increasing development pressures, the impacts of globalization, and [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change). More subtle threats include creeping suburbanization and [horsiculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_equestrian_terms#H).[[2]](#cite_note-AONB_story-2)

[Poet Laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet_Laureate_of_the_United_Kingdom) [Simon Armitage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Armitage) wrote a poem "Fugitives", commissioned by the National Association of AONBs, which he read on [Arnside Knott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnside_Knott) on 21 September 2019 to launch the celebration of the 70th anniversary of the [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949).[[30]](#cite_note-aonb-fugitives-30)[[31]](#cite_note-ecologist-31)[[32]](#cite_note-fugitives-32)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:England_and_Wales_National_Landscapes_map.svgNational Landscapes in [England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_and_Wales)

A National Landscape ([Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_language): Tirwedd Cenedlaethol), formally and formerly an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB; [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_language): Ardal o Harddwch Naturiol Eithriadol, AHNE), is one of 38 areas of [countryside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_area) in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England) and [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales) that has been designated for [conservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_area) due to its significant landscape value. The current name was adopted in 2023.

Areas are designated in recognition of their national importance by the relevant public body: [Natural England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_England) or [Natural Resources Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_Resources_Wales), respectively. On 22 November 2023, following a review, the AONBs in England and Wales adopted the National Landscapes name, and are in the process of rebranding. The name "area of outstanding natural beauty" is still the designated legal term.

[Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland) has eight areas that maintain the name "[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty_(Northern_Ireland))", as the renaming did not apply to Northern Ireland which is under different legislation. Scotland uses the similar [national scenic area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_scenic_area_(Scotland)) (NSA) designation.

National Landscapes enjoy levels of protection from development similar to those of [UK national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_the_United_Kingdom), but unlike national parks the responsible bodies do not have their own [planning powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_and_country_planning_in_the_United_Kingdom). They also differ from national parks in their more limited opportunities for extensive outdoor recreation.[[1]](#cite_note-Gov-1)

There are 38 National Landscapes, 33 wholly in England, [four wholly in Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Landscapes_in_Wales) and [one on the England–Wales border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wye_Valley_National_Landscape), as well as a further eight AONBs in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland).

The idea for what would eventually become the AONB designation was first put forward by [John Dower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Gordon_Dower) in his 1945 Report to the Government on National Parks in England and Wales. Dower suggested there was need for protection of certain naturally beautiful landscapes that were unsuitable as national parks owing to their small size and lack of wildness. Dower's recommendation for the designation of these "other amenity areas" was eventually embodied in the [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949) as the AONB designation.[[2]](#cite_note-AONB_story-2)

The purpose of an AONB designation in England and Wales is to [conserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landscape-scale_conservation) and enhance the natural beauty of the designated landscape.[[1]](#cite_note-Gov-1)

There are two secondary aims: meeting the need for quiet enjoyment of the countryside and having regard for the interests of those who live and work there. To achieve these aims, AONBs rely on [planning controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_and_country_planning_in_the_United_Kingdom) and practical countryside management. As they have the same landscape quality, AONBs may be compared to the [national parks of England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_England_and_Wales). National parks are well known in the UK; by contrast, there is evidence to indicate many residents in AONBs may be unaware of the status. However, the National Association of AONBs launched initiatives to increase awareness of AONBs in local communities,[[3]](#cite_note-3) and, in 2014, successfully negotiated to have the boundaries of AONBs in England shown on [Google Maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Maps).[[4]](#cite_note-4)

## Statistical overview
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=National_Landscape&action=edit&section=3)]

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ThreeCliffsBay.jos.500pix.jpgView over [Three Cliffs Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Cliffs_Bay) in the [Gower Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gower_Peninsula), the first designated Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty
There are 48 "Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty" in the United Kingdom in total, 33 in England, [four in Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areas_of_Outstanding_Natural_Beauty_in_Wales), [one on the England–Wales border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wye_Valley_AONB), and a further eight AONBs in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland). Those in England and Wales are branded as "National Landscapes".

The first AONB was established in 1956 on the [Gower Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gower_Peninsula) in [South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Wales), and the most recent to be designated is the [Tamar Valley AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamar_Valley_AONB), established in 1995.[[5]](#cite_note-5) More recent changes include the Clwydian Range AONB being extended in 2012 to form the [Clwydian Range and Dee Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clwydian_Range_and_Dee_Valley) AONB, and in Northern Ireland, the [Strangford Lough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangford_Lough) and [Lecale Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale_Coast_AONB) AONBs were merged to form a single AONB in 2010.[[6]](#cite_note-strangfordandlecale-6)

AONBs vary greatly in terms of size, type and use of land, and whether they are partly or wholly open to the public. The smallest AONB is the [Isles of Scilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isles_of_Scilly), 16 km2 (6.2 sq mi), and the largest is the [Cotswolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotswolds),[[7]](#cite_note-7) 2,038 km2 (787 sq mi). AONBs cover around 15% of England and 4% of Wales.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

## Legal status and organisation
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=National_Landscape&action=edit&section=4)]

Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in [England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_and_Wales) (now also National Landscapes) were originally created under the same legislation as the [national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park), the [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949). Unlike AONBs, national parks have special legal powers to prevent unsympathetic development. AONBs in general remain the responsibility of their local authorities by means of special committees that include members appointed by a [minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_(United_Kingdom)) and by parishes, and only very limited statutory duties were imposed on local authorities within an AONB by the original 1949 Act. However, further regulation and protection of AONBs in England and Wales was added by the [Countryside and Rights of Way (CRoW) Act 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countryside_and_Rights_of_Way_Act_2000), under which new designations are now made,[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

In the [National Planning Policy Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Planning_Policy_Framework) (March 2012), the government stated that AONBs and national parks have equal status when it comes to planning decisions on landscape issues. Two of the AONBs (the Cotswolds and the Chilterns), which extend into a large number of local authority areas, have their own statutory bodies, known as conservation boards. In 2019, the [Glover Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Glover_(journalist)) made various recommendations regarding the future of AONBs – the report's 'central proposal' being to bring [National Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_the_United_Kingdom) and AONBs together as part of one 'family of national landscapes'.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Following the report the Cotswolds Conservation Board announced in September 2020 that they were re-styling the area name and it is now known as the Cotswolds National Landscape.[[12]](#cite_note-12) The UK Government later accepted the report's recommendation for the AONBs in England to use "National Landscape".[[13]](#cite_note-13)

All English and Welsh AONBs have a dedicated AONB officer and other staff. As required by the CRoW Act, each AONB has a management plan that sets out the characteristics and special qualities of the landscape and how they will be conserved and enhanced. The AONBs are collectively represented by the "National Landscapes Association",[[14]](#cite_note-14) previously the "National Association for Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty" (NAAONB), an independent registered charity in England and Wales[[15]](#cite_note-15) acting on behalf of AONBs and their partners, which had used the slogan "Landscapes for Life".[[16]](#cite_note-aaonb-16)

AONBs in Northern Ireland are designated under separate legislation, originally under the Amenity Lands (NI) Act 1965; later replaced by the Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (NI) Order 1985.[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-:19-18)[[19]](#cite_note-:2-19) The [Northern Ireland Environment Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Environment_Agency) (part of the [Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Agriculture,_Environment_and_Rural_Affairs)[[20]](#cite_note-20) of the [Northern Ireland Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Executive)) is responsible for designating AONBs in Northern Ireland, and facilitates their management.[[21]](#cite_note-:7-21)

On 22 November 2023, following a 2022 Landscapes Review policy paper by [Julian Glover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Glover_(journalist)),[[22]](#cite_note-22) the AONBs in England and Wales adopted the National Landscapes name, and subsequently rebranded.[[23]](#cite_note-nlwelcome-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24) The name "area of outstanding natural beauty" is still the designated legal term.[[25]](#cite_note-25) The review did not extend to Northern Ireland, and its AONBs did not adopt the new name.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Amexstadjuly10.jpg[Falmer Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falmer_Stadium) under construction in 2010 in the former [Sussex Downs AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex_Downs_AONB)
There are growing concerns among environmental and countryside groups that AONB status is increasingly under threat from development. The [Campaign to Protect Rural England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_to_Protect_Rural_England) said in July 2006 that many AONBs were under greater threat than ever before.[[27]](#cite_note-27) Three particular AONBs were cited: the [Dorset AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorset_AONB) threatened by a road plan, the threat of a football stadium in the [Sussex Downs AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex_Downs_AONB), and, larger than any other, a £1 billion plan by [Imperial College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_College_London) to build thousands of houses and offices on hundreds of acres of AONB land on the [Kent Downs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_Downs) at [Wye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wye,_Kent).[[28]](#cite_note-28) The plan was eventually abandoned in 2006 after sustained local opposition. However, in September 2007 government approval was finally given for the development of a new football ground for [Brighton and Hove Albion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton_and_Hove_Albion) within the boundaries of the Sussex Downs AONB, after a fierce fight by conservationists. The subsequent development, known as [Falmer Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falmer_Stadium), was officially opened in July 2011. The Weymouth Relief Road in Dorset was constructed between 2008 and 2011, after environmental groups lost a High Court challenge to prevent its construction.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

Writing in 2006, Professor Adrian Phillips listed threats facing AONBs, which he says include uncertainty over future support for land management, increasing development pressures, the impacts of globalization, and [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change). More subtle threats include creeping suburbanization and [horsiculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_equestrian_terms#H).[[2]](#cite_note-AONB_story-2)

[Poet Laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet_Laureate_of_the_United_Kingdom) [Simon Armitage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Armitage) wrote a poem "Fugitives", commissioned by the National Association of AONBs, which he read on [Arnside Knott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnside_Knott) on 21 September 2019 to launch the celebration of the 70th anniversary of the [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949).[[30]](#cite_note-aonb-fugitives-30)[[31]](#cite_note-ecologist-31)[[32]](#cite_note-fugitives-32)

Map of the eight Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in Northern Ireland

An Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB) in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland), is an area of countryside that has been designated for [statutory protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_area), due to their significant landscape value, by the [Northern Ireland Environment Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Environment_Agency). There are eight AONBs in Northern Ireland; [Antrim Coast and Glens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antrim_Coast_and_Glens), [Binevenagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binevenagh), [Causeway Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causeway_Coast), [Lagan Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley), [Mourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourne_AONB), [Ring of Gullion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Gullion), [Sperrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperrins), and [Strangford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangford_Lough) and [Lecale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale_Coast_AONB).

Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in Northern Ireland are designated under the [Amenity Lands Act (Northern Ireland) 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenity_Lands_Act_(Northern_Ireland)_1965?action=edit&redlink=1) or the [Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (NI) Order 1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_Conservation_and_Amenity_Lands_(NI)_Order_1985?action=edit&redlink=1). Lagan Valley AONB is the oldest designated AONB in Northern Ireland designated in 1965, it is also the smallest, while Sperrin AONB is the largest AONB. The newest change was in 2010, when Strangford Lough and [Lecale Coast AONBs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale_Coast_AONB) were merged as the Strangford and Lecale AONB.

It shared the name with a similar designation used in [England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_and_Wales), until 2023 when those areas adopted the "[National Landscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Landscape)" terminology, although their legal name still remains AONB.

The [Amenity Lands Act (Northern Ireland) of 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenity_Lands_Act_(Northern_Ireland)_1965?action=edit&redlink=1) was passed.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) Soon after, in 1965, the [Lagan Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley) AONB was designated.[[2]](#cite_note-:9-2) In 1966, the [North Derry AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Derry_AONB) and parts of south [Armagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Armagh) were designated.[[3]](#cite_note-:4-3)[[4]](#cite_note-:10-4) In 1967, the [Lecale Coast AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale_Coast_AONB) was designated.[[5]](#cite_note-:11-5) In 1968, the [Sperrin AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperrin_AONB) was designated.[[6]](#cite_note-:12-6)

In 1972, the [Strangford Lough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangford_Lough) AONB was designated.[[7]](#cite_note-:13-7)

The [Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (NI) Order of 1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_Conservation_and_Amenity_Lands_(NI)_Order_1985?action=edit&redlink=1) was passed, replacing the 1965 legislation as the main basis for AONB designation.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1)[[8]](#cite_note-:19-8)

Under the new legislation, in 1986, the [Mourne AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourne_AONB) was designated.[[9]](#cite_note-:14-9) In 1988, the [Antrim Coast and Glens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antrim_Coast_and_Glens) AONB was designated.[[10]](#cite_note-:15-10) In 1989, the [Causeway Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causeway_Coast) AONB was designated.[[11]](#cite_note-:16-11) In 1991, the [Ring of Gullion AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Gullion_AONB) was designated,[[12]](#cite_note-:17-12) covering the parts of south Armagh that had already been designated in 1966.[[4]](#cite_note-:10-4)

Also in the 1990s, there were two proposed AONBs, both in [County Fermanagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Fermanagh), [Erne Lakeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lough_Erne) and [Fermanagh Caveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble_Arch_Caves).[[13]](#cite_note-:8-13) The [Environment and Heritage Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment_and_Heritage_Service) of the Department of the Environment conducted wide consultations for the proposals in 1996–1997, with the reception being mixed.[[14]](#cite_note-:3-14)

In 2003, the Northern Ireland Environment Agency published "Shared Horizons", setting out government policy on Northern Ireland's landscapes, including Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty. It outlines the value of AONBs for more than just scenery but also their cultural heritage, biodiversity and economic benefits.[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15)

In 2006, the [Binevenagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binevenagh) AONB was re-designated replacing the North Derry AONB and with larger borders.[[3]](#cite_note-:4-3) In 2010, the Strangford AONB and the [Lecale Coast AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale_Coast_AONB) were merged into the Strangford and Lecale AONBs.[[16]](#cite_note-:18-16)[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15) By 2014, seven of the eight AONBs in Northern Ireland, were designated or re-designated under the 1985 order, except the [Lagan Valley AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley_AONB) which remains under the 1965 act.[[17]](#cite_note-:20-17)

In November 2023, Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in England and Wales adopted the branding of "National Landscapes" following a review by [Julian Glover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Glover_(journalist)), although the legal designation there still remains as an "Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty".[[18]](#cite_note-18) However, such review did not extend to Northern Ireland, therefore AONBs in Northern Ireland were not renamed as "National Landscapes", but occasionally are grouped with the equivalent designation in England and Wales.[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-:0-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

Management of an AONB differs for each AONB, but fall into three forms (as of June 2020):[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15)

- Local authorities (one or multiple) manage the Ring of Gullion, and Strangford Lough and Lecale AONBs, in line with how AONBs are managed in England and Wales.

- Charitable trusts manage the Mourne, Causeway Coast, Binevenagh and Antrim Coast and Glens.

- There is no formal management body for Sperrin, but a joint statement for planning is provided through the Sperrins Forum.

Lagan Valley Regional Park Ltd oversees the Lagan Valley AONB. It is the sole AONB that remains designated under the previous legislation.[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15)

Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in Northern Ireland are designated under either the [Amenity Lands Act (Northern Ireland) 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenity_Lands_Act_(Northern_Ireland)_1965?action=edit&redlink=1) or the later [Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (NI) Order 1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_Conservation_and_Amenity_Lands_(NI)_Order_1985?action=edit&redlink=1).[[8]](#cite_note-:19-8)[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) Landscapes with a distinctive character may be designated as an AONB based on the quality of their landscapes, heritage and wildlife, as well as their recreational value. The Planning Strategy for Rural Northern Ireland 1993 is used to set out planning policies to be applied to development proposals.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) Of the current eight AONBs in Northern Ireland, all except the [Lagan Valley AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley_AONB) (as of 2014), were designated or re-designated under the 1985 order.[[17]](#cite_note-:20-17)

The designation of "Area of outstanding natural beauty" differs between the two pieces of legislation. Those designated under the 1965 act focus on planning controls within their designated areas, while those under the 1985 order focus on the positive management of their designated areas. Areas designated under the 1965 act do not cease to be AONBs following the repeal of the act, unless re-designated under the 1985 order. Following the passing of the 1985 order, the [Department of the Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_the_Environment_(Northern_Ireland)) intended to re-designate all of the AONB from the 1965 act to be under the 1985 order. By 2003, it had re-designated the Mourne, Causeway Coast, Antrim Coast and Glens, and the Ring of Gullion AONBs.[[14]](#cite_note-:3-14) The 1985 order also allows the designation for the first national park in Northern Ireland.[[14]](#cite_note-:3-14) The [Northern Ireland Environment Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Environment_Agency) (part of the [Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Agriculture,_Environment_and_Rural_Affairs)[[22]](#cite_note-22) of the [Northern Ireland Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Executive)) is responsible for designating AONBs in Northern Ireland, and facilitates their management.[[23]](#cite_note-:7-23)

Article 14 of the Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (Northern Ireland) Order 1985 sets out the objectives for AONB designation, in principle. For an area to be designated as an AONB, the agency may develop proposals that:[[24]](#cite_note-:1-24)

- Conserve or enhance the natural beauty or amenities of an area

- Conserve wildlife, historic objects or natural phenomena of an area

- Promote public's enjoyment of the area

- Provide or maintain public access to the area

The agency would utilise an AONB designation to increase awareness for the "outstanding qualities" of the designated area and seek to ensure that the special qualities of the area are recognised and result in tangible achievements for the area's conservation. The Northern Ireland Executive's departments and [district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Districts_of_Northern_Ireland) councils have a statutory duty to have regard for the conservation needs of the area's natural beauty and the amenity of the countryside. The department will also assess whether particular policies or activities affect the conservation and well-being of an AONB, while also encouraging and assisting where it can under a co-ordinated conservation approach.[[24]](#cite_note-:1-24)

AONBs are classed under [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature) [Category V of protected areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_protected_area_categories), a "Protected Landscape/Seascape".[[14]](#cite_note-:3-14)[[25]](#cite_note-25) They are the largest and most well-known landscape designation in Northern Ireland.[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15)

Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty cover 20–24% of Northern Ireland's land area,[[20]](#cite_note-:0-20)[[23]](#cite_note-:7-23)[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15) and about 70% of its coastline.[[26]](#cite_note-26) The eight areas are:[[27]](#cite_note-27)

- [Antrim Coast and Glens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antrim_Coast_and_Glens) AONB – Designated in 1988, covering the coastline of [County Antrim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Antrim), from [Ballycastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballycastle,_County_Antrim) to [Larne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larne).[[10]](#cite_note-:15-10) It also includes [Rathlin Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rathlin_Island),[[28]](#cite_note-28) and is dominated by the [Antrim Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antrim_Plateau).[[29]](#cite_note-29)

- [Binevenagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binevenagh) AONB – Designated in 2006, but a re-designation, replacing the [North Derry AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Derry_AONB) which was designated in 1966.[[3]](#cite_note-:4-3) It covers an area between the [Roe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Roe) estuary and [Magilligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magilligan), covering Binevenagh mountain, the [Bann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Bann) estuary, and the sand dunes of [Portstewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portstewart).[[30]](#cite_note-30)

- [Causeway Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causeway_Coast) AONB – Designated in 1989, and covers the [Giant's Causeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant), Northern Ireland's sole [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site).[[11]](#cite_note-:16-11) It covers 18 miles (30 km) of coastline.[[31]](#cite_note-:5-31)

- [Lagan Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley) AONB – Designated in 1965, and mainly lies within the [Lagan Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley) Regional Park (the park itself designated in 1967). It centres on the [River Lagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Lagan) and close to the [Belfast metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast_metropolitan_area).[[2]](#cite_note-:9-2)

- [Mourne AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourne_AONB) – Designated in 1986, it covers the [Mourne Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourne_Mountains). Within it are the twelve peaks of the range, including [Slieve Donard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slieve_Donard), Northern Ireland's highest mountain standing at 850 metres (2,790 ft),[[9]](#cite_note-:14-9) as well as [Slieve Croob](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slieve_Croob). It also covers 25 miles (40 km) of coastline.[[31]](#cite_note-:5-31)[[32]](#cite_note-32)

- [Ring of Gullion AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Gullion_AONB) – Designated in 1991, it surrounds the mountain of [Slieve Gullion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slieve_Gullion) which sits at the centre of the AONB. Circling the mountain is a ring of lower rugged hills known as the [Ring of Gullion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Gullion), which give the AONB its name and is one of the most known [ring dykes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_dyke) in the [British Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles), and the first one in the world to be geologically mapped.[[12]](#cite_note-:17-12)

- [Sperrin AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperrin_AONB) – Designated in 1968, covering mountainous areas, from the [Strule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Strule) valley in the west towards the [Lough Neagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lough_Neagh) lowlands in the east. It is the largest AONB in Northern Ireland. It was redesignated in 2008, increasing its size from 101,000 hectares (390 sq mi; 1,010 km2) to 118,206 hectares (456.40 sq mi; 1,182.06 km2) to cover foothills in the north of the AONB. It is named after and covers the [Sperrins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperrins) mountain range of Northern Ireland, and the range's various valleys and uplands.[[6]](#cite_note-:12-6)

- [Strangford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangford) and [Lecale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale) AONB – Designated in 2010, the follows the shores of [Strangford Lough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangford_Lough) and up the [River Quoile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Quoile), the town of [Downpatrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downpatrick) and towards the [Irish Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Sea) coast.[[16]](#cite_note-:18-16) It was formed from the merger of the Strangford Lough AONB (designated in 1972[[7]](#cite_note-:13-7)) and the Lecale Coast AONB (designated in 1967[[5]](#cite_note-:11-5)).[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15)

Map of the eight Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in Northern Ireland

An Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB) in [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland), is an area of countryside that has been designated for [statutory protection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_area), due to their significant landscape value, by the [Northern Ireland Environment Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Environment_Agency). There are eight AONBs in Northern Ireland; [Antrim Coast and Glens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antrim_Coast_and_Glens), [Binevenagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binevenagh), [Causeway Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causeway_Coast), [Lagan Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley), [Mourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourne_AONB), [Ring of Gullion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Gullion), [Sperrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperrins), and [Strangford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangford_Lough) and [Lecale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale_Coast_AONB).

Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in Northern Ireland are designated under the [Amenity Lands Act (Northern Ireland) 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenity_Lands_Act_(Northern_Ireland)_1965?action=edit&redlink=1) or the [Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (NI) Order 1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_Conservation_and_Amenity_Lands_(NI)_Order_1985?action=edit&redlink=1). Lagan Valley AONB is the oldest designated AONB in Northern Ireland designated in 1965, it is also the smallest, while Sperrin AONB is the largest AONB. The newest change was in 2010, when Strangford Lough and [Lecale Coast AONBs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale_Coast_AONB) were merged as the Strangford and Lecale AONB.

It shared the name with a similar designation used in [England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_and_Wales), until 2023 when those areas adopted the "[National Landscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Landscape)" terminology, although their legal name still remains AONB.

The [Amenity Lands Act (Northern Ireland) of 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenity_Lands_Act_(Northern_Ireland)_1965?action=edit&redlink=1) was passed.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) Soon after, in 1965, the [Lagan Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley) AONB was designated.[[2]](#cite_note-:9-2) In 1966, the [North Derry AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Derry_AONB) and parts of south [Armagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Armagh) were designated.[[3]](#cite_note-:4-3)[[4]](#cite_note-:10-4) In 1967, the [Lecale Coast AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale_Coast_AONB) was designated.[[5]](#cite_note-:11-5) In 1968, the [Sperrin AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperrin_AONB) was designated.[[6]](#cite_note-:12-6)

In 1972, the [Strangford Lough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangford_Lough) AONB was designated.[[7]](#cite_note-:13-7)

The [Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (NI) Order of 1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_Conservation_and_Amenity_Lands_(NI)_Order_1985?action=edit&redlink=1) was passed, replacing the 1965 legislation as the main basis for AONB designation.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1)[[8]](#cite_note-:19-8)

Under the new legislation, in 1986, the [Mourne AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourne_AONB) was designated.[[9]](#cite_note-:14-9) In 1988, the [Antrim Coast and Glens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antrim_Coast_and_Glens) AONB was designated.[[10]](#cite_note-:15-10) In 1989, the [Causeway Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causeway_Coast) AONB was designated.[[11]](#cite_note-:16-11) In 1991, the [Ring of Gullion AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Gullion_AONB) was designated,[[12]](#cite_note-:17-12) covering the parts of south Armagh that had already been designated in 1966.[[4]](#cite_note-:10-4)

Also in the 1990s, there were two proposed AONBs, both in [County Fermanagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Fermanagh), [Erne Lakeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lough_Erne) and [Fermanagh Caveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble_Arch_Caves).[[13]](#cite_note-:8-13) The [Environment and Heritage Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment_and_Heritage_Service) of the Department of the Environment conducted wide consultations for the proposals in 1996–1997, with the reception being mixed.[[14]](#cite_note-:3-14)

In 2003, the Northern Ireland Environment Agency published "Shared Horizons", setting out government policy on Northern Ireland's landscapes, including Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty. It outlines the value of AONBs for more than just scenery but also their cultural heritage, biodiversity and economic benefits.[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15)

In 2006, the [Binevenagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binevenagh) AONB was re-designated replacing the North Derry AONB and with larger borders.[[3]](#cite_note-:4-3) In 2010, the Strangford AONB and the [Lecale Coast AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale_Coast_AONB) were merged into the Strangford and Lecale AONBs.[[16]](#cite_note-:18-16)[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15) By 2014, seven of the eight AONBs in Northern Ireland, were designated or re-designated under the 1985 order, except the [Lagan Valley AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley_AONB) which remains under the 1965 act.[[17]](#cite_note-:20-17)

In November 2023, Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in England and Wales adopted the branding of "National Landscapes" following a review by [Julian Glover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Glover_(journalist)), although the legal designation there still remains as an "Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty".[[18]](#cite_note-18) However, such review did not extend to Northern Ireland, therefore AONBs in Northern Ireland were not renamed as "National Landscapes", but occasionally are grouped with the equivalent designation in England and Wales.[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-:0-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

Management of an AONB differs for each AONB, but fall into three forms (as of June 2020):[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15)

- Local authorities (one or multiple) manage the Ring of Gullion, and Strangford Lough and Lecale AONBs, in line with how AONBs are managed in England and Wales.

- Charitable trusts manage the Mourne, Causeway Coast, Binevenagh and Antrim Coast and Glens.

- There is no formal management body for Sperrin, but a joint statement for planning is provided through the Sperrins Forum.

Lagan Valley Regional Park Ltd oversees the Lagan Valley AONB. It is the sole AONB that remains designated under the previous legislation.[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15)

Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty in Northern Ireland are designated under either the [Amenity Lands Act (Northern Ireland) 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenity_Lands_Act_(Northern_Ireland)_1965?action=edit&redlink=1) or the later [Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (NI) Order 1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_Conservation_and_Amenity_Lands_(NI)_Order_1985?action=edit&redlink=1).[[8]](#cite_note-:19-8)[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) Landscapes with a distinctive character may be designated as an AONB based on the quality of their landscapes, heritage and wildlife, as well as their recreational value. The Planning Strategy for Rural Northern Ireland 1993 is used to set out planning policies to be applied to development proposals.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) Of the current eight AONBs in Northern Ireland, all except the [Lagan Valley AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley_AONB) (as of 2014), were designated or re-designated under the 1985 order.[[17]](#cite_note-:20-17)

The designation of "Area of outstanding natural beauty" differs between the two pieces of legislation. Those designated under the 1965 act focus on planning controls within their designated areas, while those under the 1985 order focus on the positive management of their designated areas. Areas designated under the 1965 act do not cease to be AONBs following the repeal of the act, unless re-designated under the 1985 order. Following the passing of the 1985 order, the [Department of the Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_the_Environment_(Northern_Ireland)) intended to re-designate all of the AONB from the 1965 act to be under the 1985 order. By 2003, it had re-designated the Mourne, Causeway Coast, Antrim Coast and Glens, and the Ring of Gullion AONBs.[[14]](#cite_note-:3-14) The 1985 order also allows the designation for the first national park in Northern Ireland.[[14]](#cite_note-:3-14) The [Northern Ireland Environment Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Environment_Agency) (part of the [Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Agriculture,_Environment_and_Rural_Affairs)[[22]](#cite_note-22) of the [Northern Ireland Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Executive)) is responsible for designating AONBs in Northern Ireland, and facilitates their management.[[23]](#cite_note-:7-23)

Article 14 of the Nature Conservation and Amenity Lands (Northern Ireland) Order 1985 sets out the objectives for AONB designation, in principle. For an area to be designated as an AONB, the agency may develop proposals that:[[24]](#cite_note-:1-24)

- Conserve or enhance the natural beauty or amenities of an area

- Conserve wildlife, historic objects or natural phenomena of an area

- Promote public's enjoyment of the area

- Provide or maintain public access to the area

The agency would utilise an AONB designation to increase awareness for the "outstanding qualities" of the designated area and seek to ensure that the special qualities of the area are recognised and result in tangible achievements for the area's conservation. The Northern Ireland Executive's departments and [district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Districts_of_Northern_Ireland) councils have a statutory duty to have regard for the conservation needs of the area's natural beauty and the amenity of the countryside. The department will also assess whether particular policies or activities affect the conservation and well-being of an AONB, while also encouraging and assisting where it can under a co-ordinated conservation approach.[[24]](#cite_note-:1-24)

AONBs are classed under [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature) [Category V of protected areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_protected_area_categories), a "Protected Landscape/Seascape".[[14]](#cite_note-:3-14)[[25]](#cite_note-25) They are the largest and most well-known landscape designation in Northern Ireland.[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15)

Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty cover 20–24% of Northern Ireland's land area,[[20]](#cite_note-:0-20)[[23]](#cite_note-:7-23)[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15) and about 70% of its coastline.[[26]](#cite_note-26) The eight areas are:[[27]](#cite_note-27)

- [Antrim Coast and Glens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antrim_Coast_and_Glens) AONB – Designated in 1988, covering the coastline of [County Antrim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Antrim), from [Ballycastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballycastle,_County_Antrim) to [Larne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larne).[[10]](#cite_note-:15-10) It also includes [Rathlin Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rathlin_Island),[[28]](#cite_note-28) and is dominated by the [Antrim Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antrim_Plateau).[[29]](#cite_note-29)

- [Binevenagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binevenagh) AONB – Designated in 2006, but a re-designation, replacing the [North Derry AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Derry_AONB) which was designated in 1966.[[3]](#cite_note-:4-3) It covers an area between the [Roe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Roe) estuary and [Magilligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magilligan), covering Binevenagh mountain, the [Bann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Bann) estuary, and the sand dunes of [Portstewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portstewart).[[30]](#cite_note-30)

- [Causeway Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causeway_Coast) AONB – Designated in 1989, and covers the [Giant's Causeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant), Northern Ireland's sole [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site).[[11]](#cite_note-:16-11) It covers 18 miles (30 km) of coastline.[[31]](#cite_note-:5-31)

- [Lagan Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley) AONB – Designated in 1965, and mainly lies within the [Lagan Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagan_Valley) Regional Park (the park itself designated in 1967). It centres on the [River Lagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Lagan) and close to the [Belfast metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast_metropolitan_area).[[2]](#cite_note-:9-2)

- [Mourne AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourne_AONB) – Designated in 1986, it covers the [Mourne Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourne_Mountains). Within it are the twelve peaks of the range, including [Slieve Donard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slieve_Donard), Northern Ireland's highest mountain standing at 850 metres (2,790 ft),[[9]](#cite_note-:14-9) as well as [Slieve Croob](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slieve_Croob). It also covers 25 miles (40 km) of coastline.[[31]](#cite_note-:5-31)[[32]](#cite_note-32)

- [Ring of Gullion AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Gullion_AONB) – Designated in 1991, it surrounds the mountain of [Slieve Gullion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slieve_Gullion) which sits at the centre of the AONB. Circling the mountain is a ring of lower rugged hills known as the [Ring of Gullion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Gullion), which give the AONB its name and is one of the most known [ring dykes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_dyke) in the [British Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles), and the first one in the world to be geologically mapped.[[12]](#cite_note-:17-12)

- [Sperrin AONB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperrin_AONB) – Designated in 1968, covering mountainous areas, from the [Strule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Strule) valley in the west towards the [Lough Neagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lough_Neagh) lowlands in the east. It is the largest AONB in Northern Ireland. It was redesignated in 2008, increasing its size from 101,000 hectares (390 sq mi; 1,010 km2) to 118,206 hectares (456.40 sq mi; 1,182.06 km2) to cover foothills in the north of the AONB. It is named after and covers the [Sperrins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sperrins) mountain range of Northern Ireland, and the range's various valleys and uplands.[[6]](#cite_note-:12-6)

- [Strangford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangford) and [Lecale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecale) AONB – Designated in 2010, the follows the shores of [Strangford Lough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangford_Lough) and up the [River Quoile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Quoile), the town of [Downpatrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downpatrick) and towards the [Irish Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Sea) coast.[[16]](#cite_note-:18-16) It was formed from the merger of the Strangford Lough AONB (designated in 1972[[7]](#cite_note-:13-7)) and the Lecale Coast AONB (designated in 1967[[5]](#cite_note-:11-5)).[[15]](#cite_note-:6-15)
